title: Acute Heart Failure and Pulmonary Oedema
clinicalScenario: A 68-year-old with known ventricular dysfunction reports three days of worsening breathlessness, new orthopnoea, and ankle swelling after a respiratory illness. They are tachypnoeic and cannot lie flat. The case asks the learner to assess perfusion and oxygenation, distinguish congestion from competing acute causes, and plan safe escalation.

pathophysiology.summary: Raised filling pressures cause pulmonary or systemic venous congestion; impaired output and neurohormonal activation can worsen renal sodium retention. Acute triggers may include ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled blood pressure, medication interruption, or renal deterioration. This scenario is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

impaired output and neurohormonal activation can worsen renal sodium retention. Acute triggers may include ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled blood pressure, medication interruption, or renal deterioration.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis

title: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State
clinicalScenario: A 77-year-old with type 2 diabetes presents after several days of thirst, poor intake, and increasing confusion during a febrile illness. They are markedly dehydrated. Infection, impaired access to fluids, medicines, and vascular illness are common contributors. This scenario is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

Benefit and safety depend on age, comorbidity, immune status, prior doses, exposure, and current national recommendations. This scenario is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

clinicalScenario: A 33-year-old at 28 weeks develops unilateral leg swelling and pleuritic breathlessness after prolonged immobility. The learner must assess for DVT/PE, choose pregnancy-appropriate diagnostic imaging, and balance anticoagulation, bleeding, delivery, and neuraxial considerations.

Thromboembolism threatens maternal oxygenation and requires coordinated diagnostic and anticoagulation planning. title: Last Days of Life Care
clinicalScenario: A 79-year-old with advanced cancer is bedbound, taking little fluid, and has fluctuating consciousness. Family asks whether they should continue routine medicines and artificial hydration. The learner must recognise possible dying while considering reversible causes, comfort, communication, and family support.

pathophysiology.summary: Physiological decline near death may involve reduced intake, consciousness, mobility, and organ function. These changes can be distressing but vary; clear communication and repeated symptom review support comfort and family understanding. This scenario is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
